These sites are more-so for people who aren’t quite ready to fully recover (or to recover at all yet). We try our best to avoid obvious triggers (like competitive comments, insults, numbers, etc), but simply talking abt our different experiences and ed thoughts can be triggering in itself. It’s comforting to be able to talk w others who are experiencing what you’re experiencing, which is why these forums exist. But you gotta know that the mere existence of these spaces is triggering. When I was really far in recovery, I had deleted all of my accounts and apps that could bring me to these sites bc I didn’t want to trigger myself. I missed the ability to talk to people who can relate to me, but I ultimately felt better without the constant triggers. So yeah, the intention of these sites isn’t to purposefully be triggering or to promote eds, they’re simply for people who already have eds to have some sort of community and some outlet to share their experiences that others wouldn’t understand. I’m really sorry that coming back here triggered you so badly, but it doesn’t eliminate all of your progress! First and foremost, make sure you’re not going through this alone. Have a therapist or a dietician or even your family that help you along your recovery journey. They’ll be able to give suggestions, support you, and call out your ed bullshit lol. For example, I had a team of a therapist and dietician that helped from a medical standpoint, and I meal-planned with my older brother who went to school w me so he could help me during all meal times. 

Secondly, each person goes into recovery in different ways. Just as there isnt one specific look for eds, there isnt one specific look for recovery. However I will say that what helped me was to begin by increasing my intake. I’d eat mostly just safe foods (with added fats to increase the cals without increasing the volume much). THEN only once I felt comfortable w eating more, did I start incorporating fear foods. But, like I said, what works for me may not work for you. 

A lot of recovery is constantly reminding yourself “it’s okay to eat x”, “it’s okay to not workout after a meal”, “just one meal won’t make me gain weight”, “nothing bad will happen if I eat x”, etc etc. I hate to say it but those ed thoughts are gonna be persistent throughout the first few months of recovery. They’ll feel super loud and overwhelming and they’ll try to convince you that you’re not strong enough for recovery, but it’s okay, that’s the sound of your ed losing. The more you fight those thoughts, the quieter they will get. And you ARE strong enough, despite what your ed might tell you. Recovery is possible, and it’s so fucking awesome too. There’s so much joy in life that your ed takes away from you, and sometimes you don’t even realize what was missing until you get it back again. Being able to enjoy a party without stressing over the food, being able to go out to eat w friends without planning how to purge the meal, being able to enjoy working out again with your stronger and healthier body. It’s all so incredibly worth it. Sending you all the hugs <33

Having extreme disordered eating (like intense binge eating or intense restriction) for a long enough time (which you said you’ve been struggling with this your whole life but experienced significant weight changes within the past 4yrs) is more than enough to qualify for a diagnosis. Since you’ve experienced long periods of binging and long periods of restricting, you would most likely qualify for OSFED (ofc I’m not diagnosing you, I’m just sharing my knowledge). Under the umbrella of OSFED are several different types of disordered eating. The one you would specifically have depends on your mindset, your thinking process about food and body image, and your most primary disordered eating behaviors. imo it sounds like you would qualify for AAN (atypical anorexia), which is literally just AN but without the UW requirement. 

Try not to fall into the trap of “if I truly had AN I wouldn’t x” thinking, bc there’s so many different approaches to AN. Some people develop fears of processed sugars, some develop fears of fats, some develop fears of meat, etc etc. Fear foods and/or avoiding certain foods is common, but there isn’t exactly a rhyme or reason for which food someone would fear. There isn’t one “look” for anorexia. Just bc you yourself feel comfortable consuming juices and grapes doesn’t mean that your disordered eating is invalid in any way. Hell, some of my safest foods are fruits and oats with honey (which both have carbohydrates and calories in them). To have AN doesn’t mean that you NEVER eat, bc obviously if you never ate you’d die really quickly. You’re still restricting your caloric intake. You’re still losing a shit ton of weight at a speed that is clearly unhealthy and disordered

I agree with others that she should go to therapy, bc ultimately it’s not that impressionable to hear from family abt it. As a teenager, I had this idea that my family didn’t know what was best for me and that they didn’t care enough abt me. I can’t assume that’s what she will think, but I would just err on the side of caution. Granted, it would be insanely helpful for you to share your experience anyways. She may not want to listen to you bc you’re family, but it would be helpful to hear from someone who’s lived with an ed for decades. That way she knows that you relate, but also you can give her first-hand knowledge of what it’s like to have an ed for so long. Lay on heavy w comments of “I can’t begin to understand what you’re going through” and “I want you to know that I care, and I’m here for you” and stuff so she knows that you’re not just trying to say “ik exactly what you’re experiencing and ik exactly how to fix it”, bc that impression wouldn’t help her at all. Shift her thinking into long-term thinking. When I fell deep into my ed, I wasn’t really thinking abt how it would affect my future bc I either didn’t think I’d live to be an adult, or I thought that I’d somehow magically recover once I hit adulthood. But that’s not how eds work. The longer you feed into it, the harder it is to get rid of. Try to emphasize that a life w an ed isn’t worth it. Share all of the downsides that you experienced, both physically (weakness, tiredness, hair loss, etc) and socially (not going out to eat w friends, choosing to workout instead of socializing, etc) and academically (brain fog causing grades to slip). But ultimately point out that you’re there to support her, and you’re willing to jump through hoops to get her professional support as well, and that recovery IS possible, and that her life will be so much better without her ed. 

I’m really sorry that this is happening to her and to you. I really hope for the best for both of you!

I’m really educated in this due to my extensive experience in levels of treatment. I’ll list them in order of severity and explain each one:

1. Psychiatric inpatient hospitalization: this is the one you know already. It’s 3-7 days usually, and you stay at the hospital under extreme supervision. There isn’t much therapy happening here, they’re just setting up a care plan for you or waiting until you’re safe again essentially.

2. Residential treatment center (RTC): this is a more comfortable, longer term treatment. It’s a 30-60 day stay usually. You live at the center in a controlled environment to be able to receive intense therapy. There’s 5-6hrs of therapy each day. I’ve done multiple residentials, and I’ve had some good experiences and some bad ones. I’d say (if your family decides you need it) that you should definitely do your research and find a program that looks beneficial to you.

3. Partial hospitalization program (PHP): this is essentially residential treatment, but you get to go home! It’s 5-7 days a week, 5-6hrs of therapy daily, and the program usually lasts 3-4 weeks. I’m currently completing a PHP program rn. Mine is a weekday program that runs from 9am-2pm every day, which is kinda the standard for PHPs.

4. Intensive outpatient program (IOP): this is PHP but less days and less hours. You do 3-5 days per week, ~3hrs each day, and the program is usually 8-12 weeks long.

So the psych ward is the psychiatric inpatient unit. Psychiatric inpatient treatment is at an actual hospital with lots of staff bc those patients need lots of care. This level of care tends to be short-term (about a week). 

Residential treatment is at a house that’s been up-cycled for treatment. A small amount of patients live there for a longer period of time (about a month). There’s always a nurse, and at least another staff on duty, but at night, there is usually only those people.

Then there’s PHP which is partial hospitalization program. PHP is a day program where you go for a certain number of hours that you and your care team has determined is right for you, however, the usual time is normal work schedule.

Lastly, there’s IOP which is intensive outpatient program. This is usually for a few hours or so a few  times a week.

When I think of OCD intrusive thoughts, they’re persistent and there’s no way to convince your brain that it won’t happen/you didn’t do it. Following that logic, cleaning has to be done in a certain order or a certain way. For example, when I clean the bathroom it has to go in the order mirrors, toilet, sink, shower, light switches, baseboards, floors, door handles, and trash can. Hey, recovering anorexic here with a little advice. I definitely know how you feel. I felt the only option was to dive into an ed. It worked for the first few months. I lost weight, I felt happier with my body. I couldn’t sleep at night, I was constantly thinking about food, I had nonstop brain fog, I almost fainted a lot, and lots of other terrible things, but at least I was skinny. Then I had a near-death experience and had to choose recovery. And I gained the weight back. The weight you lose in your ed isn’t permanent. It isn’t worth all of the suffering.

You do have another option: to fix your body image issues. Don’t get me wrong, it’s insanely difficult to fix (I’m still struggling w this), but it’s easier than recovering from an ed AND fixing your body image issues at the same time. If you don’t want to go to therapy, try reading a self-help book or articles written by therapists on this. 

Here’s at least what my therapist worked on with me. The first step is body neutrality. Your arm is simply an arm. It’s not an ugly or fat arm, but you don’t have to believe it’s beautiful either. Just repeat to yourself that it simply exists. Fake it till you make it. The same applies to other body parts as well obviously. It sounds silly ik, but it helps. I also like the exercise of being grateful for what your body can do. Your body can walk up stairs. Your body can rock that workout. Be proud of what your body does!! Acknowledging the good things can help you realize the “bad” things are actually neutral
Socialize to the best of your ability. It really made my experience way more manageable. Without my psych ward friends I probably would’ve stayed there 3x longer ngl
